newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq faces new sanctions from UN Council.
newsitem.headline: Iraq faces new sanctions from UN Council.

text.p: The United Nations Security Council has unanimously warned Iraq it faced further sanctions if it did not allow U.N. arms inspectors to search sensitive sites.

The late Saturday 15-0 vote on a resolution came after a deal was struck between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russia's Boris Yeltsin at the Group of Seven summit of industrial states in Denver that averted a Russian veto.

China's vote had been in doubt until the last minute while its envoys consulted with Beijing on the document drafted by the United States and Britain and co-sponsored by Chile, Costa Rica, Japan, Poland, Portugual and Sweden.

U.N. inspectors, looking for weapons of mass destruction and related materials documents, were prevented from searching three sites on June 10 and 12. Iraq argued it had could bar them from areas dealing with national security.
Unless the inspectors are satisfied, stringent sanctions against Iraq, particularly oil exports, cannot be lifted. The embargoes were imposed in 1990 after Baghdad invaded Kuwait.
"There is less poison than there was before but it is still poisonous," said Iraq's ambassador Nizar Hamdoon before the vote was taken. "That's my way of describing the text."

The resolution, however, postpones differences in the council until October when, in the words of British Ambassador Sir John Weston, "it points firmly towards taking additional measures against Iraq."

But a new resolution would be needed to impose any further sanctions, such as a travel ban on Iraqi officials responsible for blocking the inspections. Egypt, Russia and China have indicated they had reservations on enacting new sanctions.

Although the final text was weaker than the United States and Britain first proposed, both nations were satisfied that the council took a tougher position than it has over the last year. Russia had threatened to veto their original text while France would have abstained.
Specifically, the resolution:
-- expresses the council's "firm intention to impose additional measures" on Iraqi officials responsible for barring the U.N. arms inspectors from sensitive sites.
-- suspends regular reviews until October of trade sanctions imposed on Iraq, usually held every 60 days. On Oct. 11 the inspectors report again on Iraqi compliance.
-- condemns Iraq's action and demands unconditional access for U.N. arms inspectors to all areas as well as officials and others they want to interview.
Weston also said Iraq's actions were "part of a clear pattern of concealment, harassment and obstruction" and "obviously directed from the highest levels in Baghdad."

U.S. representative Edward Gnehm said Iraq for the past two years had intensified efforts to "conceal its true weapons capabiities, destroy evidence on its programmes and supply routes and lie about it to this council."
He warned that "the day cannot come when sanctions relief is in sight" unless Iraq cooperated with the council.

A senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Yeltsin had agreed to "accept the principle of new sanctions" after his conversation with Clinton in Denver on how to prevent "rogue states seeking to develop weapons of mass destruction."
Their meeting was followed up by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who spoke to Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and French Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine.

Originally the United States and Britain wanted immediate travel sanctions on the military as well as certain government departments responsible for barring U.N. inspectors from three sensitive sites last week. But Russia, China, France and Egypt opposed punitive measures and Moscow threatened a veto.

Russia's U.N. ambassador Sergei Lavrov, repeatedly stressed to reporters that the new text imposed no new sanctions. He said the United States and Britain had wanted to introduce a range of sanctions "that would cover even secretaries and cleaners and the like."
But he said "this resolution is to send a strong signal from the council" to make sure U.N. inspectors could complete their work and the oil embargo could be lifted.
